procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 16.06.2009 of the High Court of Karnataka at Bangalore in R.P.F.C. No. 103 of 2008 and 21 of 2009.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court set aside the order of the family court and held that appellant No.1 was unable to prove that she is the legally wedded wife of the respondent. The High Court further held that she has not produced any evidence to show that the marriage was solemnized as per custom and she, not being the legally wedded wife, is not entitled for any maintenance.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Kamala and Others (Appellants) approached the Supreme Court after the High Court overturned the Family Court's order. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in its revisional jurisdiction, is empowered to reassess the evidence and substitute its own findings of fact for those of the trial court.

facts: The family court, after considering oral and documentary evidence, found that a valid marriage existed between the parties.
In a revisional proceeding, the High Court set aside the family court's order.
The High Court's reasoning was that the appellant had not sufficiently proven that she was the legally wedded wife of the respondent.
law: A High Court, when acting in its revisional jurisdiction, does not have the power to reassess evidence and substitute its own views on findings of fact for those made by the trial court.
In proceedings for maintenance under Section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.), strict proof of marriage is not a necessary requirement.
application: The Supreme Court applied the principle that revisional jurisdiction is limited. It found that the family court had already made a finding of fact regarding the existence of a valid marriage based on the evidence presented.
The Supreme Court determined that the High Court overstepped its authority by re-evaluating this evidence to arrive at a different conclusion.
Furthermore, the Court noted that the High Court failed to consider the lower standard of proof required for marriage in a Section 125 Cr.P.C. proceeding, which is not as stringent as in other cases.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had improperly exercised its revisional jurisdiction. It held that the High Court should not have interfered with the factual findings of the family court, and therefore rejected the proposition that a High Court has the power to reassess evidence and substitute its own findings in such a capacity.

issue.issue_text: Whether strict proof of marriage is a prerequisite for claiming maintenance under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

facts: A woman and her two children claimed maintenance under Section 125 CrPC from the respondent, whom she claimed was her husband.
The respondent denied the marriage and his paternity of the children.

The Family Court granted maintenance, finding sufficient proof of marriage based on the wife's testimony, the children's birth certificates, photos, and witness statements from a co-worker and landlord.
The High Court set aside the Family Court's order, holding that the woman had failed to provide strict proof that she was the legally wedded wife of the respondent.
law: Proceedings under Section 125 of the CrPC are summary in nature and are intended to prevent vagrancy.
Unlike in matrimonial proceedings (e.g., for divorce), a strict standard of proof of marriage is not necessary for a maintenance claim under Section 125.
The law presumes in favour of marriage and against concubinage when a man and a woman have cohabited continuously for a number of years.
The term “wife” under Section 125 should be given a broad and expansive interpretation to fulfill the provision's beneficial purpose of upholding social justice and individual dignity.
application: The Court determined that the evidence of the couple living together as husband and wife, having two children, and being treated as a married couple by their community was sufficient for a Section 125 proceeding.
It applied the legal presumption of a valid marriage based on the long-term cohabitation of the parties.
The Court found that the Family Court had correctly applied this lower standard of proof to the evidence.

It concluded that the High Court erred by acting as a revisional court to reassess the evidence and by incorrectly applying the strict standard of proof required for matrimonial cases, not for summary maintenance proceedings.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that strict proof of marriage is a prerequisite for claiming maintenance under Section 125 CrPC. It held that because these are summary proceedings designed to prevent destitution, a lower standard of proof applies, and a presumption of marriage arises from long-term cohabitation. Therefore, the Court overturned the High Court's decision and reinstated the Family Court's order granting maintenance.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in its revisional jurisdiction, is empowered to reassess the evidence and substitute its own findings of fact for those of the trial court.
appellant_arguments: The High Court, in exercising its revisional jurisdiction, ought not to have interfered with the findings of fact recorded by the family court, which were based on an analysis of the evidence on record.

arguments.issue_text: Whether strict proof of marriage is a prerequisite for claiming maintenance under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
appellant_arguments: When parties live as husband and wife under one roof, a presumption arises in favour of the person asserting the existence of a valid marriage.
Since the parties entered into a wedlock in a temple, lived together, and had two children, a presumption of marriage arises which the respondent failed to rebut.
respondent_arguments: Under Section 125 (1)(a) Cr.P.C., an application for maintenance can be maintained only by a “wife” who is a legally wedded wife.
No valid marriage had taken place between appellant No.1 and the respondent and hence, appellant No.1 is not entitled to claim any maintenance under Section 125 Cr.P.C.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In proceedings for maintenance under Section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code, strict proof of marriage is not a necessary precondition.
obiter: A broad and expansive interpretation should be given to the term “wife” to include cases where a man and woman have been living together as husband and wife for a reasonably long period of time.
Where a man and woman are proved to have lived together as man and wife, the law will presume, unless the contrary is clearly proved, that they were married.
A revisional court does not have the power to reassess evidence and substitute its own views on findings of fact established by a lower court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court held that for the purpose of claiming maintenance under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the term "wife" must be given a broad and expansive interpretation. This interpretation includes cases where a man and woman have been living together as husband and wife for a reasonably long period. Consequently, requiring strict proof of marriage as a precondition for granting maintenance is contrary to the spirit and essence of this beneficial provision.
legal_tests_applied: A broad and expansive interpretation should be given to the term “wife” to include even those cases where a man and woman have been living together as husband and wife for a reasonably long period of time, and strict proof of marriage should not be a precondition for maintenance under Section 125 CrPC.
policy_considerations: A broad interpretation of "wife" is necessary to fulfil the true spirit and essence of the beneficial provision of maintenance under Section 125.
Such an interpretation would be a just application of the principles enshrined in the Preamble to our Constitution, namely, social justice and upholding the dignity of the individual.
